name: Ada Lovelace
title: The Visionary
tagline: She translated a paper about a machine that was never built, and her long Notes showed what computers might one day do.

fourmilab.label: Sketch of the Analytical Engine, with Notes by the Translator, A. A. L. (1843), full text at Fourmilab

babbage-passages.label: Charles Babbage, Passages from the Life of a Philosopher (1864), Project Gutenberg #57532

chm.label: Ada Lovelace, The Babbage Engine (Computer History Museum)

principles.title: Look past the numbers
principles.idea: Babbage built his engines to calculate. Ada saw something bigger: if the rules of a subject could be written as symbols, the machine could work on that subject too, even music. This is the idea behind every computer today.

quote.text: ...the engine might compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity or extent.
quote.credit: Notes on Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine, Note A (1843)

principles.practice: Pick a tool you use every day. Write down one thing it could do that it was not built for.

principles.title: Explain with a good picture
principles.idea: To show how the engine worked, Ada compared it to the Jacquard loom, which used punched cards to weave patterns into cloth. One clear comparison made a strange new machine easy to imagine.

quote.text: We may say most aptly, that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves.
quote.credit: Notes on Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine, Note A (1843)

principles.practice: Think of something you know well that others find hard. Explain it to a friend using one comparison to something everyday.

principles.title: Be honest about limits
principles.idea: Ada warned readers not to overrate the engine. It could only do what people knew how to tell it to do. Being clear about what a tool cannot do is part of understanding it. Alan Turing argued with this line more than a hundred years later.

quote.text: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.
quote.credit: Notes on Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine, Note G (1843)

principles.practice: Next time you are excited about a new idea or tool, write one honest line about what it cannot do.

principles.title: Work out every step
principles.idea: Note G ends by tracing, step by step, how the engine could compute the Bernoulli numbers. Babbage later wrote that when he offered to do this part for her, she found a serious mistake in his work and sent it back to be fixed.

quote.text: We will terminate these Notes by following up in detail the steps through which the engine could compute the Numbers of Bernoulli...
quote.credit: Notes on Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine, Note G (1843)

principles.practice: Take one task you do by habit. Write out every step in order, then check each step for a mistake.

principles.title: Spot what repeats
principles.idea: In her Notes, Ada named a group of steps that is done again and again a cycle. Seeing what repeats lets you write it once and use it many times, which is how programmers think about loops today.

quote.text: A cycle of operations, then, must be understood to signify any set of operations which is repeated more than once.
quote.credit: Notes on Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine, Note E (1843)

principles.practice: Find one job you repeat every week. Write its steps once as a short checklist you can reuse.

challenge.title: Beyond its purpose
challenge.action: Pick one everyday tool. Write down one new thing it could do if someone used it differently.

challenge.title: One good picture
challenge.action: Explain something you know well to a friend using one comparison to something everyday.

challenge.title: Every step
challenge.action: Write out, step by step, how you do one task you usually do without thinking.

challenge.title: Check the work
challenge.action: Go back over yesterday's steps, or something you made this week, and look for one mistake to fix.

challenge.title: Find the cycle
challenge.action: Spot one set of steps you repeat often. Turn it into a short checklist you can reuse.

challenge.title: Honest limits
challenge.action: Pick an idea you are excited about. Write one clear line about what it cannot do.

challenge.title: Your own notes
challenge.action: Like Ada, add your own notes to something you read this week: what it means and where it could lead.

reflect: What is one thing you use every day that could do far more than it was built for, if someone imagined it?
